q: Calculate the mitotic index near the tip and 2 cm from the tip.
Explain the difference between the two regions.
The tip contains meristem cells that divide repeatedly; further back the cells have stopped dividing and are elongating and differentiating.
Describe and explain the effect of colchicine.
Many cells are stuck in metaphase (70) and none are in anaphase or telophase. Without a spindle, chromosomes line up but the chromatids cannot be pulled apart, so cells cannot leave metaphase.
The cell cycle near the tip lasts 20 hours. Estimate the time spent in metaphase.
12 / 180 × 20 h = 1.3 h (about 80 minutes).
Suggest why cells should be counted in several fields of view.
One field may not be representative; more fields give a more reliable mean.
Calculate how many times greater the risk is at 40 than at 30.
Describe the trend.
Low and almost steady up to about 30, then rising more and more steeply after 35.
Explain how trisomy 21 arises.
Non-disjunction in meiosis: the two chromosome 21s (or chromatids) fail to separate, so an egg gets two copies; fertilisation adds a third.
Suggest why the risk rises with the mother’s age.
Eggs are held part-way through meiosis I from before birth; over decades the proteins holding chromosome pairs together deteriorate, so separation errors become more likely.
Most babies with trisomy 21 are born to mothers under 35. Suggest why, despite the lower risk.
Far more babies are born to younger mothers, so a small risk applied to many births gives more cases.
